body_markdown:
*Timothy* writes:


Sajeev,


I have[another Piston Slap](https://www.hagerty.com/media/advice/piston-slap/piston-slap-save-this-honda-element-again/) for you! This one stems from a comment that I made on an article posted a few weeks ago on Hagerty, when your fellow writer Stefan Lombard[initially stated](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/3-winners-and-3-losers-from-the-classic-chevy-market/#comments:~:text=Chevy%E2%80%99s%20Monte%20Carlo,moniker%20in%201982.) that the ’78-’80 Monte Carlo and the ’81-’89 were entirely different cars. I commented that this wasn’t the case, that it was a mid-cycle refresh and a name change (A-body to G-Body), but otherwise it was the same car. The article was amended, somewhat, but it left me with lingering questions.


1978 Monte Carlo


Chevrolet


1980 Monte Carlo


Chevrolet


1981 Monte Carlo (Turbo)


Chevrolet


When is a car a “new generation”? I contend that the ’78-’89 Monte Carlo was the same car, much like the B-Body Caprice was the same car from ’77 through ’90. However, I would argue that the Panther platform cars went through such significant changes between ’91 and ’92 that they were “new” cars, or at least a half-model difference.


This could go on ad infinitum—the ’38 VW Type 1 is almost an entirely different car than the 2000-era South American “Fusca,” but it’s often lumped together. The ’09 Model T and the ’27 Model T are significantly different…but similar enough to be the “same” car? *Please weigh in!*


*Sajeev* answers:


Funny you mention it, as I was the person who “somewhat amended” that Monte Carlo story you read. It was a moment when brevity is the preferred choice to keep on-topic. Thankfully, Piston Slap is not a place for quick corrections, and there are two terms that help answer your question: Mid-Cycle Refresh and a Clean-Sheet Design. *(The latter term is the answer to your question.)*


## The Mid-Cycle Refresh


The 1983-86 Mercury Cougar C-pillar.


Mercury


The 1987-88 Mercury Cougar C-pillar.


Mercury


The mid-cycle refresh makes mild-to-moderate cosmetic changes (a redesigned roof pillar, new door cards, new front and rear fascias), and/or just about any functional upgrade (powertrain, chassis, suspension, brakes, electronics) under the skin. The intention is to add a dash of modernity to an older design, ensuring a modicum of freshness before a fully new design reaches production.


Your G-body Monte Carlo reference is one such example, as it did the mid-cycle refresh correctly in 1981, much like my favorite example: The 1986 vs. 1987 Mercury Cougar. Both the Monte and the Cougar elevated the mid-cycle refresh to include redesigned roof pillars. The G-body received a[colonnade treatment](https://www.hagerty.com/media/hagerty-marketplace/in-the-oldsmobile-cutlass-rocket-powered-muscle-collided-with-malaise-engineering/comment-page-2/#:~:text=1958)%20Flickr%20%7C%20leonelponce-,GM%E2%80%99s%20A%2Dbody%20platform%20and%20its%20various%20sedans%2C%20wagons%2C%20and%20%E2%80%9C,Oldsmobile,-The%20Cutlass%E2%80%99%20styling) , while the Cougar received enlarged and flush-mounted side glass. But the Cougar also received convex rear glass, which must have been pricey to implement, considering how many cars today prefer flat glazing at the rear.


A clean-sheet design has more than a new face and a pair of new roof pillars. There should be an entirely different roof, *and that’s just for starters.*


## A Truly Clean-Sheet Design


Volkswagen


You mentioned the VW Type-1, and I reckon it’s the only truly clean-sheet design in the era of mass-produced automobiles. There were a lot of automotive startups in the early days making cars from scratch—or from horse-drawn carriages—but those feel irrelevant to modern car production.


But speaking of startups, the 2013 Tesla Model S comes very close to the Beetle, even if it shared smaller components with Diamler-Benz (switchgear) and Ford (throttle pedal). Both the Beetle and the Model S required Herculean amounts of money and labor to create from scratch, but we can probably add some flexibility to the definition of a clean-sheet design.


A clean sheet must look significantly different from every angle, both inside and outside. The look should translate into different[volumes](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-a-glossary-of-automotive-design-terms/#:~:text=Volumes%3A%20The%20basic%20shape%20of%20a%20vehicle%2C%20the%C2%A0outline%20of%20the%20body%20work%20when%20seen%20from%20the%20side.%20More%20info%20here.) for each space (hood, passenger seating, and cargo) to prove the body was indeed altered from the previous generation.


1988 Cutlass Supreme Classic


Oldsmobile


1988 Cutlass Supreme


Oldsmobile


For simplicity’s sake, let’s stick to a single vehicle nameplate over time, ignoring tectonic shifts like the 1993 Dodge Intrepid to its Dynasty predecessor. While the cab-forward LH cars were fantastic, a clean sheet shouldn’t necessarily wipe out the outgoing nameplate. And with that, your mention of the G-body is actually a good place to start. The traditional G was instantly obsolete when the GM-10 (or W-body) personal luxury coupes from any vantage point.


Even postwar icons of “newness” like the 1949 Ford can’t touch this transition, as one peek under the hood proved Ford retained the L-head six and flathead V-8 from pre-war models. The GM-10’s drove a different set of wheels, had a new V-6 engine (only new to this platform), possessed rocket-ship styling inside and out, and sported new proportions that redefined the personal luxury coupe.


Opening any portal shows new volumes, tighter under the hood and somewhat cavernous in the passenger and cargo compartments. This has been the trend over the past 40 years of automotive history, but the GM-10 was probably the most aggressive clean-sheet design of any nameplate.


1988 Cougar


Mercury


1989 Cougar


Mercury


Sticking with the modern classic era of this question, the[GM-10](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/when-the-buick-regal-failed-to-put-a-w-in-gms-corner-it-was-too-late/) of the Cutlass Supreme/Regal and the[MN-12](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/a-v-8-couldnt-save-fords-directionless-mn12-platform/) in the Thunderbird/Cougar are probably my high watermarks for clean-sheet redesigns. Both possessed a shocking lack of interchangeability with their predecessor, but at least the Ford retained its rear-wheel-drive layout. A clean sheet shouldn’t mandate cutting off one’s nose to spite its face!


But I am just a singular car enthusiast, with a specific opinion of “what makes a new vehicle new.” What do you think, dear reader?
